summary: Warns that protocols such as ARP and Neighbor Discovery carry link-layer addresses whose bit order differs between LAN technologies. Implementors must take care to use the canonical form so that all parties interpret the bits the same way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: LAN hardware does not always place address bits in memory in the same order. This memo explains canonical order and where implementations may need to swap bits for correct interpretation.

subtitle: A warning that link-layer address bits may be ordered differently by LAN hardware.

tldr.problem: Some LAN adapters represent link-layer address bits in memory in a different order from canonical form.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines canonical order and explains when implementations or bridges may need to bit-swap address bytes.
tldr.outcome: Fields that require canonical form must be handled in that form; bridges between Token Ring and Ethernet swap ARP address bits.

today: RFC 2469 is an Informational memo published in December 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Address Ordering Matters
sections.content:
ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery carry link-layer addresses in message fields. To interoperate, a sender must ensure that the receiver extracts and interprets those bits correctly. In most cases, these fields must use canonical form.

LAN adapters are not consistent in how they represent canonical form. Implementations may need to swap bits within individual bytes when moving addresses to or from an adapter.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender and receiver must interpret the same address bits in the same order. Some adapters need software to change the bit order before using an address.

sections.title: Canonical and Non-Canonical Forms
sections.content:
Canonical form, also called LSB or Ethernet format, maps the first bit sent on the LAN to the least significant bit of each byte in memory. The group address indicator is therefore the least significant bit of the first byte. Ethernet and 802.3 hardware follow this definition.

Token Ring and some FDDI hardware map the first bit to the most significant bit in memory. This is called MSB, IBM, Token-Ring or non-canonical format. For the canonical address 12-34-56-78-9A-BC, the memo shows the MSB-format bytes as 48 2C 6A 1E 59 3D.
sections.plainLanguage: Canonical form puts the first bit sent on the LAN in the least significant position in memory. Some Token Ring and FDDI adapters use the opposite order.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery, ARP and Bridges
sections.content:
The IPv6-over-link-layer documents require addresses in Neighbor Discovery options to be sent in canonical order. The authors report that Ethernet adapters use that order, while some FDDI and all Token Ring adapters appear to use non-canonical form. Implementations must send and interpret Neighbor Discovery addresses correctly for their local adapters.

ARP addresses on Ethernet use canonical order. The de facto practice on Token Ring is non-canonical order, which works between Token Ring nodes. A bridge between Token Ring and Ethernet swaps address bits in forwarded ARP packets so each network type can interpret them.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbor Discovery fields must use canonical order. Bridges between Token Ring and Ethernet swap ARP address bits when forwarding between the two network types.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it raises no known security issues. Its focus is helping implementations avoid using non-canonical forms in fields that require canonical form.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo reports no known security issues. It explains an address-format detail needed for correct interpretation.
